claim: Let \(\psi\) be a continuous convex function on \([0,1]\) with \(\psi(0)=\psi(1)=1\), \(\max\{1-t,t\}\le \psi(t)\le1\), and \(\psi(t)=\psi(1-t)\). Let \(N_\psi\) be the associated absolute normalized norm on \(\mathbb R^2\), and put \(\psi_2(t)=\sqrt{(1-t)^2+t^2}\). If either (i) \(\psi\ge\psi_2\) and \(\psi/\psi_2\) attains its maximum at \(t=1/2\), or (ii) \(\psi\le\psi_2\) and \(\psi_2/\psi\) attains its maximum at \(t=1/2\), then the Ptolemy constant and Euclidean Banach--Mazur distance satisfy \(C_{\mathrm{Pt}}(N_\psi)=d_{\mathrm{BM}}((\mathbb R^2,N_\psi),\ell_2^2)^2\). In case (i) both equal \(2\psi(1/2)^2\); in case (ii) both equal \(1/(2\psi(1/2)^2)\).

correctness.rationale: For any Euclidean pullback H, scaling gives N<=H<=dN. Squaring and averaging the quadratic form over signed coordinate permutations preserves both inequalities and forces a scalar multiple of x^2+y^2, proving the coordinate circle is globally Banach--Mazur optimal. The distortion is the midpoint ratio under the stated hypotheses. Zuo's Theorems 2.2 and 2.3 give the same midpoint ratio squared as the Ptolemy constant. All quantifiers are finite-dimensional and no numerical experiment is used.

value.rationale: The claim unifies a metric four-point invariant with an affine linear-distortion invariant on an infinite and natural class of Banach planes. It explains why several exact-value coincidences occur and replaces family-by-family ellipse optimization by one structural symmetry argument. The result is not a mere recomputation of a known table entry.
